🚀 Build with AI · Step 7 of 7 · 7 min

Run it for real users

Speed, cost, what to watch after launch, and building for failure.

⏱️ What a user feels: the first token and the last

A user waits twice. First for the time to first token (TTFT): the request reaches the model, the model reads it, and the first token appears. Then for the rest of the answer, which the model writes token by token at its generation speed, in tokens per second.

Streaming shows the text while it is being written. The total time stays the same, but the user can start reading after the first token, so the wait feels much shorter.

total time ≈ time to first token + output tokens / tokens per second
1 s to the first token, then 300 tokens at 100 per second:
1 + 300 / 100 = 1 + 3 = 4 s

A model reads the input in parallel, far faster than it writes the output token by token. So a longer input mostly adds to the time to first token.

Task. A model starts to answer after 0.5 seconds and then writes 50 tokens per second. How many seconds does an answer of 400 tokens take in total?

Show the solution

0.5 s until the first token, then 400 / 50 = 8 s of writing: 0.5 + 8 = 8.5 seconds. Here the model spends almost all of the time writing, so the wait depends mostly on the length of the answer.

Task. The same model: 0.5 s to the first token, then 50 tokens per second, and an answer of 400 tokens. Which change shortens the total time the most?

Show the answer

Right answer: Asking for answers of 200 tokens, not 400

Instead of 8.5 s, a 200-token answer takes 0.5 + 200 / 50 = 4.5 s, and half the time to the first token gives 0.25 + 8 = 8.25 s. A shorter question cuts only the time to the first token, and only a little. Streaming changes how the wait feels, not how long it is.

✂️ Three ways to pay less

The bill grows with the number of model calls and with the tokens in each call. There are three common ways to cut it, and each has its own risk.

fewer tokens: shorter instructions, fewer retrieved chunks, a limit on the length of the answer
a cache: a request that was answered before gets the stored answer, with no new call to the model
routing: easy requests go to a small, cheap model, and only the hard ones to the big one

The risks: if you cut too many tokens, the model misses what it needs or the answer is cut off. A stored answer can go out of date, and one user's private data must never reach another user from the cache. And a hard request taken for an easy one can get a weaker answer.

Task. A big model costs 10 units per 1000 requests, a small model 1 unit. You send 80% of the requests to the small model and the rest to the big one. What do 1000 requests cost now, in units?

Show the solution

800 requests go to the small model: 0.8 · 1 = 0.8 units. 200 go to the big one: 0.2 · 10 = 2 units. Together 0.8 + 2 = 2.8 units instead of 10, and the 20% sent to the big model still make up most of the bill.

Task. To save money, an application sends easy-looking requests to a smaller model, and only the rest to a big one. What is the main risk of this routing?

Show the answer

Right answer: Some hard requests are taken for easy ones and get worse answers

The choice can be wrong, and a hard request sent to the small model may get a weaker answer, often with no error message. So measure the routing on an evaluation set: its quality, not only its price. A small model is usually cheaper per token and can stream, and choosing a model typically adds little time.

Task. After routing, 1000 requests cost 2.8 units. Then you add a cache: it answers 30% of the easy requests and 30% of the hard ones, without calling a model. What do 1000 requests cost now, in units?

Show the solution

70% of both the easy and the hard requests still reach a model, so the whole bill shrinks to 70%: 0.7 · 2.8 = 1.96 units. Together, routing and the cache cut the bill from 10 units to 1.96, about a fifth of what it was. But a stored answer helps only while it is still correct.

📈 After launch, the questions change

Real users ask things that were never in your evaluation set. Documents and prices change, and the model can change too. So you keep measuring after launch.

Keep a log of requests and answers, but store only what you need and hide personal details. Read a sample every week, and turn every real failure into a new test case. Track these over time:

quality: the share of thumbs up and down, and what the weekly sample shows
waiting time: the average, and the slowest 5% of requests
cost: per request and per day
errors: failed calls, time-outs, answers that cannot be parsed

Task. What does each signal most likely mean?

Show the solution

Each signal shows where to look first. Ratings point to quality, the slowest requests to one slow step, a higher cost per request to more tokens or more calls to the big model, and a jump in failed tool calls to a changed tool. The log lets you check each guess on real requests.

🧯 Build for failure

A provider can be slow or stop working for a while, an answer can come back in the wrong format, and a model version can be retired. Plan for all of this in code from the start:

a time limit on every call, and a few retries with a growing pause
a fallback when the retries fail: another model, or an honest “please try again later”
code that checks every structured answer (such as JSON) before it is used
a pinned model version: an exact version, so the model is not replaced without your decision

Even a pinned version is usually retired one day. Test the new version on your evaluation set well before that day.

Task. An application expects JSON from a model, and about 1 answer in 100 cannot be parsed. What is the right fix?

Show the answer

Right answer: Check every answer in code, and if one fails, retry or use a fallback

An instruction in capitals may make failures rarer, and temperature zero makes answers more repeatable, but neither stops all failures. Only a check in code catches every failure, and then you retry or use a fallback. Use a structured-output mode where there is one, but keep the check. And 1 in 100 is 10 failures per 1000.

Task. Why does a careful team pin an exact model version instead of always using the newest one?

Show the answer

Right answer: A new version can behave differently and break prompts that worked

A new version can answer differently, with another format, another length or other mistakes, and prompts tuned for the old one can quietly break. So an upgrade is a decision: run the evaluation set on the new version, compare, then switch. Newer is often better overall, but not for every prompt.

Remember

  • total time ≈ time to first token + output tokens / tokens per second. Writing the answer often takes most of it. Streaming does not shorten the total, but the wait feels shorter.
  • Pay less with fewer tokens, a cache and routing. Measure the routing on an evaluation set too: a hard request sent to the small model may get a weaker answer.
  • After launch, keep a log, read a sample every week, track quality, cost, waiting time and errors, and turn every real failure into a test case.
  • Build for failure: check every structured answer in code, retry with a growing pause, keep a fallback and pin the model version.
